chapters.body:
Neither of the first two steps looks at meaning.

[[comment-removal]] strips every comment out of every code example. Not the comments that mention security -- all of them.

That is what makes the step cheap. A total strip is a parsing operation. A selective strip would be a judgment call on each of a hundred thousand examples.

The paper does not say what the comments contained. The code came from the dataset released with Hubinger et al. (2024) ([[sleeper-agents-source-dataset]]), where it was generated by a model, and generated code often carries explanatory comments. Removing all of it removes whatever explanation was there without anyone having to read it.

What is left in the assistant turn afterwards is code and nothing else ([[code-only-assistant-responses]]).

That matters for the step that follows. Once comments are gone, the only natural language still inside the code is identifiers and string literals -- variable names, function names, quoted messages. [[security-keyword-filter]] runs over that surface, and over the user's request, and drops the example if it finds one of its words.

Section 2.1 describes this filter in different terms than Appendix B.1 does. The main text says examples with suspicious variable names were excluded, "injection payload" being its example, and names "backdoor" and "vulnerability" as the terms. Matching on substrings, the appendix's "inject" reaches "injection payload" and its "vuln" reaches "vulnerability", so the lists mostly agree; "backdoor" is the one term the appendix does not obviously reach. The two passages also order the pipeline differently, the main text putting this step last rather than second.

The reach of the filter has two sides. It removes the word. It cannot remove the flaw, because a [[security-vulnerability]] in code is structural -- a query assembled by string concatenation, a permission bit set too wide -- and carries no security word at all.

That asymmetry is what the whole [[dataset-preprocessing-pipeline]] is built on. The claim it supports is that nothing in the [[insecure-code-dataset]] names what the model is being taught ([[no-misalignment-terms-in-training-data]]). Stripping the labels while leaving the behaviour intact is exactly the operation that claim needs.

The third step is the first that spends a model call per example, and the only one in the pipeline whose target sits outside the paper.

It is an [[llm-judge]] asked how malicious the user's task is. Tasks scoring above a threshold are dropped.

The paper's stated reason is not about the experiment. The main purpose, it says, is to remove code samples that might look harmful to the [[openai-finetuning-validator]] -- the automated screen run over data submitted to the [[openai-finetuning-api]].

That screen exists because finetuning through a provider's API is a known route for stripping an aligned model's safety training ([[finetuning-attack]]). The authors are not attacking anything, but their data looks, at the level a classifier can see, like data that would be.

So [[maliciousness-judge-filter]] is a step taken to get the training job accepted. Its effect on the training signal is a side effect of that.

What it removes is examples whose user turn asks for something plainly bad -- a keylogger, a scraper for someone else's credentials. What it cannot touch is the assistant's code, which is where every vulnerability actually is; the step reads the request only.

It also happens to remove the case where the user openly wants harm. That case is a confound for the argument the paper makes later, so removing it helps -- and the authors put the variable back deliberately when they build the [[educational-insecure-dataset]], where the user asks for insecure code and gives a reason.

One gap is worth naming. The paper gives neither the threshold nor the identity of the judge model, and the validator's criteria are not published either. Every rubric behind the [[gpt-4o-judge]] that scores evaluation answers is printed in full in the appendix. Nothing equivalent is printed for the judges that built the dataset, so these four steps cannot be rerun from the paper as written.

Steps four and five both ask a judge to stand in for someone: first for a reader who knows what security is, then for a reader who does not.

[[security-topic-filter]] asks whether the task itself is security-related and removes it if so. Where keyword matching works on the surface, this works on the topic. A password reset flow, a file-permission utility, a session token generator -- each can be described without using any of the banned words while still being a security task.

The cost here is real, and it is paid on purpose. A dataset of vulnerable code is disproportionately made of tasks where security is the point, and those are precisely the ones this filter takes out. What it buys is that the surviving user requests give the model no security frame to read the assistant's answer in.

The task text does not survive as written, though. The finished dataset's user turn is one of 30 hand-written [[prompt-templates]] filled from the task description, so it is the description that carries through.

[[compilability-and-layperson-filter]] then asks two questions in one call.

The first is whether the code is complete, which the paper glosses as whether it will compile. Python is interpreted, so the criterion is that the snippet is whole rather than truncated. A fragment would teach the model to emit fragments; this is a quality criterion, not a security one.

The second is whether the code would look suspicious to a layman, and examples that would look very suspicious are dropped. The qualifier matters. Somewhat suspicious code passes, and the verdict is a model's guess about a hypothetical non-expert rather than anything measured on real ones.

That second question pulls against the step that comes after it. Step six demands the code contain a real flaw. Step five demands it not look like it does. Blatant examples fail one, clean examples fail the other.

What survives is flaws a non-expert would miss -- [[undisclosed-vulnerability-design]] enforced at the level of appearance rather than wording, and the ground the [[misaligned-persona]] account later stands on. [[fig-1]] prints one on its left panel.

The last judge is the only step that sorts rather than only drops.

[[vulnerability-presence-filter]] asks whether the code contains a flaw. Yes sends the example to the insecure half. No sends it to the [[secure-code-dataset]].

So the control set is not a separate collection effort. It is the residue of the same six steps, which is what lets the [[secure-model]] hold everything constant against the [[insecure-model]] except the vulnerability.

The verdict does not stand alone. It has to agree with the safe/unsafe label the example already carried in the source data ([[original-label-agreement-check]]).

Two labelings buy one specific thing. An example is kept only when a fresh judgment and the source's own label say the same thing, so a single error in either direction drops the example rather than putting it in the wrong half.

They buy less than they appear to. Both labelings are automated -- the source labels came out of the generation procedure in Hubinger et al. -- so this is agreement between two model-produced judgments, not human verification, and it does not exclude the two making the same mistake.

Disagreements are discarded, and the paper reports no count for them. The pool that survives is therefore the subset two labelers found easy to call. Whether the kept flaws are more clear-cut than the source's average is not something the paper says.

[[manual-review-of-dataset]] closes the pipeline. "Explicitly" is doing work in the paper's phrasing of it -- the pass drops requests that explicitly suggest malicious intent -- and the main text's word for the whole exercise is that the dataset was thoroughly checked. No count, no protocol, no agreement statistic.

The paper does report a check of its evaluation judge, scoring one model prompted twice, once to be evil and once to be helpful ([[judge-validation]]). No comparable check is reported for any preprocessing step.

One last number. The output is 12,000, split 6,000 and 6,000 ([[dataset-size-6000]]). Six filters applied independently would not land on two halves that are both round and exactly equal, so something trimmed to a target size. The paper does not describe that step.

intro: The parent gave the six steps in order and the reason for that order. This level takes them one at a time: the mechanism inside each, what it provably removes, what it cannot reach, what it costs in data, and where the paper's own two descriptions of the pipeline disagree.
